content: Acrodynia is a condition that manifests with a pink discoloration of the hands and feet, accompanied by irritability, photophobia (sensitivity to light), and polyneuritis (inflammation of multiple nerves). This condition is caused by chronic exposure to mercury. In young children, the most common source of exposure is the ingestion of mercury from a broken thermometer. Symptoms of mercury toxicity may not become apparent until weeks or even months after the exposure. Signs and Symptoms Initial Signs: Patients may exhibit listlessness, drowsiness, irritability, and an increased tendency to cry. There is often a loss of appetite, which can lead to subsequent weight loss. More than 50% of affected individuals report sensitivity to light (photophobia). Generalized weakness and painful extremities are also common. Within 2-4 Weeks: The tips of the nose, fingers, and toes develop a pinkish discoloration, which progressively darkens and spreads into a net-like pattern. The hands and feet become painful, cold, cyanotic (bluish in color), erythematous (reddened), and swollen. Extreme pain and itching in the extremities often result in thickened, scratched skin due to persistent rubbing and scratching by the affected child. Hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating) with a characteristic mouse-like odor may occur, potentially leading to miliaria (sweat rash) and secondary bacterial skin infections. Inflammation, swelling, and gum erosion may develop, sometimes resulting in tooth loss. Alopecia (hair loss) and nail loss have also been reported in some cases. Clinical Characteristics Central Nervous System: Patients often display significant irritability. Extreme photophobia may cause individuals to burrow their heads or cover their eyes to block out light. Cardiovascular System: Hypertension (elevated blood pressure) and tachycardia (increased heart rate) are frequently observed. Gastrointestinal System: Stomatitis (inflammation of the mouth) is often accompanied by anorexia (loss of appetite). Colitis may occur, presenting with either diarrhea or constipation. Excessive salivation is another common symptom. Renal System: Proteinuria (presence of protein in the urine) is a common finding. In severe cases, nephrotic syndrome may progress to renal failure. Dermal Manifestations: Erythema (redness) of the palms, soles, and face is frequently observed. Edema (swelling) and desquamation (peeling) of the skin on the hands and feet are common. Pruritus (itching) is a notable symptom. Muscular/Skeletal System: Hypotonia (reduced muscle tone) may be present. Miscellaneous: Gingivitis (inflammation of the gums) is often observed. Diaphoresis (excessive sweating) is common. Paresthesia (abnormal sensations such as tingling or numbness) and generalized pain are frequently reported. Treatment The primary goal of treatment is to eliminate mercury from the body and address any fluid or electrolyte imbalances. Chelating agents, such as meso-2,3-dimercaptosuccinic acid, are used to prevent the uptake of methylmercury by erythrocytes (red blood cells) and hepatocytes (liver cells). Hemodialysis, with or without the addition of L-cysteine as a chelating agent, has been employed in patients suffering from acute renal failure due to mercury toxicity.
